Using a Raman spectrometer onboard the Perseverance rover, we report the heterogeneous distribution of organic carbon within mudstones located in an ancient river valley on Mars. Measurements of two mudstones show hundreds of organic detections, making this the most robust organic detection in Jezero crater thus far, and, to our knowledge, the only detection of macromolecular carbon on a natural rock surface on Mars. Spectra of the interior of one rock reveal an association of organics with secondary carbonate and sulfate minerals, whereas another rock exhibits an association of organics with primary silicate-­dominated matrix. Although in situ Raman analyses cannot determine whether these organics denote abiotic or biotic sources, the organic association with both depositional and diagenetic minerals and the detection of organics on the martian surface suggests that the organics observed ubiquitously at the Bright Angel outcrop may be resistant to radiation and oxidation or have been relatively recently exposed.

INTRODUCTION The Mars Perseverance rover has been exploring Jezero crater since 2021, characterizing the geology of the region, searching for signs of ancient life, and collecting samples for possible future return to Earth (1). The detection and characterization of organic carbon on Mars is a critical component of assessing whether Mars ever harbored life. The 1976 Viking lander gas chromatograph–mass spectrometry experiments marked the first in situ search for organic compounds on Mars (2). Since Viking, the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) Curiosity rover’s Sample Analysis at Mars instrument has detected organic carbon in bulk measurements of sedimentary rocks at Gale crater (3–6), and multi­ple reservoirs of organic matter have been inferred (5). In addition, laboratory analyses using Raman mapping techniques have revealed the

spatial associations between minerals and organic carbon in martian meteorites (7, 8), carbonaceous chondrites (9), and ureilite meteorites (10). Here, we report robust in situ, noncontact, spatially resolved organic carbon detections on Mars by Raman spectroscopic mapping. The organic carbon detected is located within fine-­grained sedimentary rocks and exhibits mineralogical and textural associations. In addition, we observe distinct organic carbon spectral features on natural rock surfaces and abraded surfaces that expose the interior of the rock. We analyze the Raman G-­band spatial distributions across the four targets analyzed at the “Bright Angel” outcrop, and compare the calculated Raman G-­band peak characteristics to those of meteorites, terrestrial samples, and synthetic standards to constrain the nature of the organic carbon.

The Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman and Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals (SHERLOC) instrument is a deep-­ultraviolet (DUV; 248.6 nm) Raman and fluorescence mapping spectrometer and context imager on the end of the Perseverance rover’s robotic arm (11). Monochromatic and full-­color images are obtained using SHERLOC’s two cameras, the Autofocus and Context Imager (ACI) and the Wide Angle Topographic Sensor for Operations and eNgineering (WATSON), respectively. WATSON images can be used to colorize ACI images to generate a high-­ resolution (10.1 μm/pixel) image that captures both color and texture for spectral context (11). SHERLOC generates spectral maps of organics and minerals colocated with context images to determine their spatial relationships with a spectral resolution as fine as 110 μm per pixel using DUV Raman scattering and/or fluorescence within the range of 800 to 4000 cm−1 and 265 to 355 nm, respectively (11). The Raman region between ~1350 and 1650 cm−1 covers a variety of vibrational modes associated with functional groups of organic compounds (12), including D-­ and G-­bands of macromolecular carbon (MMC), which occur at ~1350 and ~1600 cm−1, respectively [e.g., (13, 14)]. MMC is a solid, cross-­linked network of primarily reduced carbon that is resistant to chemical and thermal decomposition and is insoluble and nonlabile (12, 15, 16). MMC may have different degrees of structural order (17) and includes aromatic and aliphatic structures that may have substituted heteroatoms or functional groups. We note that, in general, the use of the term “MMC” serves to avoid implications of biogenicity, whereas the terms “kerogen” and “bitumen” typically implicate past life or a biogenic source (15). The G-­band (graphitic band) is attributed to the E2g symmetry in-­plane bond-­stretching motion of sp2 bonded C atom pairs, and the D-­band (defect/disorder band) derives from the A1g symmetry ring breathing mode of six-­member carbon rings (17). The G-­band peak position and bandwidth have been correlated to a variety of structural parameters of MMC including bond order and lattice strain (17, 18). Prior SHERLOC observations of fluorescence within rock targets on the Jezero crater floor may be attributable to organics; however, several inorganic sources with similar fluorescence signals complicate such assignments (19–21). Notably, a Raman G-­band was previously detected on the crater floor; however, this detection was limited to a single point within a SHERLOC map (20). Here, we report the detection of organics in multiple ancient riverbed rock targets with dozens of detections observed in each target. We also demonstrate positive and negative control results for calibration targets interrogated during this campaign.

Neretva Vallis, Jezero crater On mission sol 1159 (martian days elapsed since rover landing), Perseverance began exploring Neretva Vallis, an ancient river channel that served as the primary inlet to Jezero crater’s western margin (Fig. 1A). The Bright Angel outcrop, located on the northern side of the channel, features light-­toned, well-­layered rocks in contact with the topographically higher deposits of the Jezero crater Margin unit (Fig. 1, A and B). The exposed outcrop was likely deposited within the channel by fluvial or lacustrine processes, but the outcrop’s relative geologic age compared to other units in Jezero crater is not currently well constrained (22, 23). From sols 1180 to 1218, the SHERLOC instrument collected 18 spectral maps (totaling 1800 spectra) from four targets across three rocks of Bright Angel (Table 1). Targets included (i) the “Cheyava Falls” dust-­cleared natural surface, (ii) the “Apollo Temple” abrasion, (iii) the “Steamboat Mountain” abrasion, and (iv) the

“Walhalla Glades” abrasion (Fig. 1 and Table 1). The Cheyava Falls and Apollo Temple targets are ~16 cm apart on the Cheyava Falls rock within the “Beaver Falls” workspace, located near the contact with the Margin unit (Fig. 1, C and D) (23). The Steamboat Mountain target is on a darker-­toned rock adjacent to the Cheyava Falls rock at the Beaver Falls workspace and closer to the Margin unit contact (Fig. 1, C to E) (23). The Walhalla Glades target is ~111 m south of the Beaver Falls workspace (Fig. 1, B and F).

RESULTS Texture and color We define “texture” as the characteristics of rock grains, including their size, shape, and spatial arrangement. We also use color and tonal descriptors to better differentiate these fine-­grained rocks. The Cheyava Falls natural surface target is a fine-­grained mudstone (≤30-­μm grains), the average grain size of which is at or below the resolution of SHERLOC’s ACI (10.1 μm/pixel) (11). The reddish matrix contains discrete irregularly shaped spots (~0.25 to 1.2 mm), which have discontinuous black rims and pale interiors (Fig. 1G). These features are flush with the rock surface and contrast sharply with cross-­cutting, erosionally resistant whitish veins, which are observed throughout the Cheyava Falls rock (Fig. 1, D and G). The Apollo Temple abrasion (7.8-­mm abrasion depth) reveals the matrix to be fine grained with dark brown and black, silt-­ to fine sand-­sized grains (~30 to 400 μm) (Fig. 1, D and H, and fig. S1A). Veins are visible in the abrasion patch, and a large pit in the abrasion patch corresponds to a vein observed on the natural surface (fig. S1A). The Steamboat Mountain abrasion target (6.8-­mm abrasion depth) is darker toned and reveals a coarser-­grained texture consisting of medium sand to gravel-­sized grains (~425 μm to 2.5 mm) with greenish centers and light-­toned rims surrounded by a fine-­grained reddish matrix (Fig. 1, C, E, and I, and fig. S2). The Walhalla Glades abrasion target (7.0-­mm abrasion depth) exhibits a very fine-­grained light-­ toned matrix with black silt-­ to fine sand-­sized (~30 to 220 μm) grains distributed relatively homogeneously throughout the matrix (Fig. 1, F and J, and fig. S1B). Details regarding WATSON and ACI imaging observations for each target are provided in tables S1 and S2.

Minerals Each SHERLOC spectroscopy measurement at the Bright Angel out­ crop covers a 1 mm by 1 mm area, which allows for the characterization of the spatial distribution of minerals and organics (Table 1). Carbonate and sulfate detections with peak centers at ~1080 cm−1 and ~1013 to 1033 cm−1, respectively, are dispersed throughout the Apollo Temple matrix (Fig. 2, A and B, and fig. S3). A subset of Apollo Temple spectra contains a stronger ~1080-­cm−1 carbonate peak, revealing mineral heterogeneity within the target (Fig. 2A and fig. S4). Few carbonate and sulfate detections were made in the Walhalla Glades and Cheyava Falls matrices compared to Apollo Temple. Detections of a potential phosphate peak (a narrow band centered at ~970 cm−1) occur in the Apollo Temple and Walhalla Glades targets and may be associated with the dark-­toned grains at Walhalla Glades (fig. S5 and S4). Detections of phosphate are corroborated by colocated x-­ray fluorescence (XRF) scans of the same areas collected by the Planetary Instrument for X-­ray Lithochemistry (PIXL) (24). Macromolecular carbon A heterogeneously distributed Raman band with a peak center at ~1600 cm−1 was detected within the fine-­grained matrix of rocks at Bright Angel. The band is present in the mapped mean and median. We report the peak characteristics derived from the trimmed mean (mean

spectrum after removing highest and lowest 5% of values) of select spectral maps, and in some cases, in subsets of maps associated with specific Raman features (Table 2 and Fig. 2). The highest-­intensity ~1600-­cm−1 peak was observed in the sol 1217 Apollo Temple abrasion (Fig. 3B), where the spectra were acquired when the instrument was closest to the ideal focus position for Bright Angel outcrop measurements (SHERLOC focus is described in the “Spectroscopy data acquisition” section and reported in Table 1). As detailed in Materials and Methods, we considered a wide range of other potential sources of, and contributions to, the ~1600 cm−1 feature observed in the rocks of Bright Angel. We explored the possibility of instrument background, inorganic Raman peak contributions from minerals and hydration, and terrestrial organic contamination. Ultimately, we found that these alternative hypotheses cannot fully account for the observed 1600-­cm−1 feature, giving us confidence in the G-­band assignment. We conclude that MMC is the most parsimonious explanation for this feature.

Although the G-­bands at Apollo Temple show no clear association with any resolvable textural components within the rock, spatially resolved spectral variations with specific mineral phases are observed in the G-­band peaks (Fig. 2). Apollo Temple G-­bands are associated with both sulfate and carbonate mineral phases (Fig. 2, A and B), with the most intense G-­band spectra associated with strong carbonate ν1 peaks (Fig. 2A) (see the “Intensity filtering algorithm for mineral and organic spatial distribution” section for details on the identification of points with both G-­band and mineral phases within spectral maps). The G-­bands in the Walhalla Glades abrasion are associated with the lighter-­toned rock matrix and are attenuated or absent within

the dark grains associated with iron phosphate (Fig. 2C) (24). The fine-­grained matrix association is supported by the results of principal components analysis (PCA) and k-­means statistical analysis applied to the reduced spectroscopy dataset (fig. S5) (see the “Principal Components Analysis and k-­means Clustering” section of the Supplementary Text for details on the application of PCA to SHERLOC spectral data). The G-­bands at Cheyava Falls do not appear to be associated with any specific mineral or texture (Fig. 2D). We do not observe the presence of a D-­band in Bright Angel measurements. Raman spectral D-­ and G-­band peak characteristics of MMC depend on the excitation wavelength used and the carbon allotrope analyzed (14, 17, 18). The D-­band signal contains a majority contribution of its intensity from aromatic cluster sizes that are in resonance with the laser excitation. Thus, for UV excitation wavelengths, we would only expect D-­band contributions from very small aromatic units and at low intensity if present in the sample (see Raman D-­ and G-­band background in the Supplementary Text). DUV resonance with aromatic organic compounds may also explain why only a G-­band is observed in the Bright Angel

SHERLOC spectra when D-­bands are commonly observed for similar materials collected using terrestrial instruments with visible excitation. Although we cannot discount the presence of a potential D-­band, we do not observe one and, therefore, focus our discussion on analyses of the G-­band at Bright Angel. The nature of the Raman detections, with an obvious G-­band in spectral means and medians compared to the weaker signal from individual map points, is likely due to inherent sample characteristics and/or instrument-­related factors. For example, SHERLOC’s position relative to the target surface during these analyses resulted in a larger laser beam spot size (~208 μm instead of ~110 μm), translating to an approximately 35% decrease in signal. MMC in geologic samples is not possible with DUV Raman spectroscopy on Mars due to several unknown instrument and Bright Angel sample properties such as (i) uncertainty in the total scattering volume interrogated by the SHERLOC laser, (ii) matrix effects of 248 nm absorption by iron, (iii) SHERLOC focus position, and (iv) uncertainty in the size, structure, and diversity of organic compounds (32). A concentration range estimate of MMC measured in the Apollo Temple abrasion using the Mars SaU 008 meteorite calibration target aboard the Perseverance rover as a known reference is presented in the Supplementary Text to demonstrate the challenges faced and assumptions required.

DISCUSSION The noncontact, in situ spatially resolved detection of MMC on Mars with Raman spectroscopy provides an unambiguous confirmation and corroboration of previous reports of organics on Mars. Previous work used temperature-­controlled pyrolysis and combustion experiments on the Curiosity rover to reveal organics, including macromolecules, in drilled samples from Gale crater (3–6). DUV Raman

spectroscopy is highly complementary to the mass spectrometry measurements of Curiosity, yielding an independent detection of organics in a different region of Mars. SHERLOC measurements at Bright Angel mark a robust detection of spatially resolved MMC with Raman spectroscopy and, to our knowledge, the only detection of organics on a dust-­cleared, but otherwise unprepared martian surface. SHERLOC’s detection of organics in a mudstone outside of Gale crater suggests that organics may have been more than just locally present and may have been more widely available in ancient (~3.5 Gyr) lakes and rivers on Mars. Raman spectra alone cannot determine biogenicity, but emplacement and formation processes may be inferred from G-­band parameters and mineral or textural associations. Below, we consider the nature, including possible sources and alteration histories, of the MMC at Bright Angel.

G-­band mineral and textural associations G-­band spatial associations with specific minerals and textural features, together with knowledge of the rock’s deposition and alteration history, can provide contextual information on the nature of the MMC [e.g., (7, 33)]. The rocks of Bright Angel are composed of fine particulate sediment that is hypothesized to have been deposited from suspension (23, 24). The source of the sediments is currently unresolved, but the silicate mineralogy of the primary grains suggests an igneous provenance, with carbonates and sulfates representing a discrete set of minerals that mark the interaction of the primary rock or sediment with surficial or subsurface fluids. Evidence for such aqueous alteration has been previously observed in igneous martian meteorites (8, 15, 41), widely across the surface of Mars (42), and locally in Jezero crater (19, 43). Characterizing the G-­band spatial distribution and mineral and textural associations may help constrain the source and alteration history of organics at Bright Angel. Interpretation of spatially resolved G-­band spectral variability is based on analyses described in Materials and Methods. A subset of points within spectral maps exhibiting G-­bands were identified using two techniques to verify consistency: (i) a spectral feature intensity ranking algorithm and (ii) PCA and k-­means cluster analysis. G-­band peak parameters derived from a subset of points within SHERLOC Bright Angel hyperspectral maps are presented in Fig. 5 (Tables 1 and 2). The most intense G-­band spectra in the Apollo Temple abrasion are associated with a carbonate mineral phase (Fig. 2A), and the mean of these points plots closest to the abiotic carbonate-­associated G-­band in martian meteorite ALH 84001 (Fig. 5) (8, 15). There is also a G-­band association with a sulfate mineral phase (Fig. 2B), but the G-­band is less intense compared to the carbonate association (Fig. 2, A and B). The most intense G-­band spectra in the Cheyava Falls natural surface measurements do not appear to be associated with specific minerals or resolvable textures, but this is likely due to the fine-­grained nature of the rock’s matrix which is at or below the ACI resolution. In addition, observations are further complicated by the higher focus offset (1.7 to 2.2 mm) during data collection compared to other targets, which increases the size of the annular beam at the target and reduces the observed Raman spectral intensity (Table 1). The most intense G-­band spectra in the Walhalla Glades abrasion are associated with the lighter-­toned matrix, and the mean of these points plot closest to the silicified microbialites from (38). This fine-­grained textural association indicates that MMC occurs within the rock’s primary mineral matrix, which PIXL data suggest is a relatively uniform silicate mixed with carbonate and sulfate (24). SHERLOC did not detect a G-­band within the black iron phosphate-­rich grains of Walhalla Glades, and a higher iron concentration in these minerals relative to the surrounding lighter-­toned matrix (24) could attenuate the spectral response through UV absorption of the signal to undetectable levels (44). The association of MMC with both primary and secondary mineral phases suggests possible relationships with depositional and diagenetic processes. Potential MMC relationships to depositional processes include the following: (i) the MMC originated from the igneous protolith sediment, or (ii) during sediment deposition in the lake (25), organic matter in the water column was incorporated between the settling sediments and lithified concurrently with the mudstones. In addition, or alternatively, MMC may have been deposited during one or more diagenetic events involving subsurface fluids. Potential MMC relationships to diagenetic events include the following: (i) early stage diagenetic fluids that facilitated the infiltration

and emplacement of organic matter into the silicate-­dominated matrix, (ii) diagenetic fluids related to the precipitation of carbonate and/or sulfate phases may have mobilized organic matter from an unknown source and simultaneously deposited it with the mineral(s), or (iii) organic matter may have been introduced during late-­stage diagenesis—post carbonate and sulfate precipitation—linking it with both primary and secondary minerals. It remains uncertain how many diagenetic events altered the mudstones of Bright Angel and what order they occurred in, or if the same diagenetic fluids altered the Cheyava Falls and Walhalla Glades rocks. While these scenarios offer insights, none conclusively identify the source of the MMC, and only speculate on the potential timing of its emplacement.

G-­band detections on a dust-­cleared mudstone The detection of G-­bands on the Cheyava Falls rock’s dust-­cleared surface represents the shallowest detection of MMC on Mars. SHERLOC’s penetration depth is dependent on the material analyzed and can be more than 500 μm in martian laboratory analogs (11, 45); however, the majority of Raman scattered photons originate from shallower depths. The surface of Mars experiences factors destructive to organics that include oxidants produced by atmospheric photochemical processes, charged particle radiation, and solar UV ≥190 nm (46, 47). While charged particles can reach depths of several meters (46), UV photons only penetrate the top several millimeters (48), making UV degradation a relevant factor regarding the surface detection on the Cheyava Falls rock. The nature of the organic material as originally formed and deposited may be significantly different from the organics observed at present by SHERLOC, following billions of years of martian geologic history. For example, MMC can form through diagenesis and catagenesis, combined with radiolysis from cosmic rays (49, 50). These processes may have transformed abiotic short-­chain alkanes and alkenes, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, carboxylic acids, amino acids, or other functionalized soluble molecules into the highly aromatized MMC observed on Mars today (51). Protective and stabilizing factors, including dust cover, photoprotective minerals, and the structure of the MMC itself, can prevent or slow UV degradation of organics; these factors are discussed below. The MMC at the Bright Angel outcrop may have been sufficiently shielded by iron-­rich regolith, which reduced exposure to UV radiation (45, 52) and atmospheric oxidation (47), and may only have been relatively recently exposed through aeolian erosion and exhumation. Martian regolith cover, although possibly transient and varying in thickness over geologic time, may need only to be 100 μm thick to offer partial UV radiation shielding (45), and 1 to 2 mm thick for more substantial shielding (53). Regolith shielding may have been thick enough to reduce UV-­oxidation products such as atmospheric H2O2 that reach the surface or near surface (micrometers to millimeters) of the Bright Angel rocks. However, because of limited numerical models, the estimated diffusion depth of atmospheric H2O2 into regolith is poorly constrained and may range from a few centimeters to hundreds of meters [(47) and references therein] and consequently does not constrain the regolith thickness necessary for preservation. In addition, photodegradation may be further inhibited by organic-­mineral interactions, as often observed when organic molecules are adsorbed onto clays—the minerals found in mudstones like Cheyava Falls—which can provide mechanical shielding by enclosing organic molecules inside the mineral’s interlayer spaces [(54) and references therein].

Last, it may be possible that the type of MMC at Bright Angel has a significantly longer lifetime in the Martian ambient environment. For example, the MMC in the SaU 008 meteorite calibration target aboard the Perseverance rover has a G-­band measured by SHERLOC that has persisted over hundreds of sols (55). Notably, the detection of macromolecules on Mars (3) and in surface particles returned from asteroid Ryugu (57) suggests that macromolecules are more recalcitrant and less likely to undergo degradation from both charged particle and short-­wavelength UV irradiation compared to more labile molecules. It is also possible that the organic matter detected on the rock surface is distinct from that detected 7.8 mm below the surface on the abrasion due to differences in organic degradation at different depths. However, the high uncertainty of the Bright Angel G-­band peak parameters, resulting from the noisy nature of the spectra due to operational conditions at the time of data acquisition (see Table 1 and Materials and Methods), precludes this evaluation, and we are therefore unable to characterize organic alteration as a function of depth on the Cheyava Falls rock.

Comparisons to other SHERLOC observations In the subsequent sections, we compare SHERLOC observations at Bright Angel to other mudstone targets and a previous G-­band detection (20) in Jezero crater. Jezero delta fan front Mudstones were previously encountered at the delta fan front within the “Shenandoah” formation (58, 59). Two abraded mudstones were analyzed by SHERLOC: “Berry Hollow” (sol 513) at the “Wildcat Ridge” outcrop and “Uganik Island” (sols 614 to 620) at the “Hidden Harbor” outcrop. Out of 600 spectral points across six maps within the Berry Hollow abrasion, and 800 spectral points across eight maps within the Uganik Island abrasion, no obvious G-­bands were observed in either rock (60). Bright Angel and Shenandoah are both sedimentary mudstones; however, their mineralogy and composition are different. Bright Angel mudstones have a silicate-­dominated matrix composed of fine-­grained aluminosilicate clays and an igneous glass and/or feldspar phase, while Shenandoah mudstones have a sulfate-­rich matrix (24, 61). The Bright Angel mudstone matrices also contain fine-­ grained carbonate and sulfate, and veins of sulfate. The Shenandoah mudstones matrices also contain Fe-­Mg phyllosilicates and sulfate veins (62). While Bright Angel clays are hypothesized products of chemical weathering, it is unclear whether Shenandoah clays are products of alteration, direct precipitates, or detrital in origin (24, 61). Assuming a primary mineral matrix, the difference in matrix and silicate composition suggests different source(s) of sediments between the two formations.

There are also notable differences in the sulfate phases between the two formations. Bright Angel is predominantly composed of Ca-­ sulfate, while Shenandoah sulfates vary in composition (Ca, Fe-­Mg, and ferric) and hydration state (24, 27, 61). At Bright Angel, anhydrous sulfate is detected in the matrix, and hydrated sulfate, consistent with bassanite, was only detected in the Steamboat Mountain abrasion where it occurs as rims around olivine grains (fig. S2). Anhydrite is detected in the matrix at Shenandoah while weakly hydrated sulfate is detected within vein interiors and rims (60). The amount and variety of sulfate phases observed in the Shenandoah formation are interpreted as evidence for sulfate formation from multi­ple fluid and/or evaporation events at the delta fan front (58, 59, 61). In addition, SHERLOC spectra show strong and pervasive sulfate-­ associated fluorescence in the Shenandoah mudstones but not at Bright Angel (60). The sulfate-­associated doublet fluorescence at 305 and 325 nm in the Shenandoah mudstones is likely due to cerium(3+) in the sulfates (21). Notably, the Shenandoah mudstones exhibit variations in doublet fluorescence intensity associated with different sulfate domains (matrix versus vein) (60). The differences observed in textures, minerals, and fluorescence between the mudstones at Neretva Vallis and the delta fan front likely record different depositional and alteration histories. Such differences suggest variation in local alteration settings instead of regional, crater-­wide alteration event(s). Jezero crater floor A G-­band was previously detected in the “Montpezat” abrasion (sol 349) at the crater floor in a single point out of 100 points in a 7 mm– by–7 mm map (20). The rock, from the “Rimplas” outcrop located in the “Máaz” formation, is an aqueously altered igneous rock dominated by pyroxene and plagioclase (1, 19). SHERLOC detected silicate, minor carbonate, and perchlorate or phosphate minerals (29). The mean spectrum of the map exhibits a relatively strong broad band centered at ~1050 cm−1, consistent with igneous glass and/or feldspar (plagioclase) (25, 29). However, the detected G-­band is colocated with a broad peak centered at ~1080 cm−1, which is consistent with carbonate, and the broadness of the feature is consistent with igneous glass and/or plagioclase (20, 25, 29). This possible spectral mix of silicate and carbonate in the rock is comparably similar to that observed in the rocks of Bright Angel, specifically Apollo Temple (Fig. 2). However, the matrix at Bright Angel and groundmass of the Máaz formation likely contain a mixture of silicate phases, making it challenging to pinpoint the specific phase associated with the G-­band. For example, the PIXL XRF maps of Montpezat reveal a mix of alkaline plagioclase feldspar, a fine-­grained KSi-­rich residual melt, and a secondary FeSi-­rich phase from serpentinized Fe-­rich olivine (29, 63). Although the G-­band association with silicate and carbonate in both the Máaz formation and Bright Angel is intriguing, it is difficult to draw conclusions based on this alone, especially considering a G-­band was detected at only a single point in the Máaz formation. In addition, the igneous Máaz formation and sedimentary Bright Angel formation both exhibit a diversity of secondary minerals, indicating that both underwent multiple aqueous alteration events. Specifically, Máaz shows evidence of olivine carbonation-­serpentinization and void-­filling salt (phosphate and perchlorate) precipitation (1, 63). In contrast, Bright Angel shows evidence of extensive vein-­filling salt precipitation (sulfate) from sulfate-­rich fluids. The relative ages of these formations and their sequence of aqueous alteration events are still unconstrained, making it challenging to speculate on organic carbon synthesis, transport, and preservation pathways.

Astrobiologically compelling sample The Bright Angel rocks within Neretva Vallis contain the most robust and ubiquitous organic detections relative to other targets that have been measured in Jezero crater by SHERLOC. These detections also represent an organic-­bearing mudstone more than 3500 km away from the detections reported from Curiosity rover measurements in Gale crater, which indicates that the habitability of Mars, and the availability of organics, may have been widespread across the planet billions of years ago. Potential organic emplacement (exogenous) and formation processes (endogenous) include the following: carbonaceous interplanetary dust particles and meteoritic infall, in situ synthesized abiotic organic matter, and/or in situ synthesized biological material. On the basis of the variety and occurrences of organic carbon in martian samples (3, 8, 16, 34, 41), there are multiple potential pathways to form abiotic organics on Mars, including condensation from igneous systems and associated volatiles, serpentinization, carbonation, and the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide in aqueous/ hydrothermal fluids (8, 41). The presence of MMC reported in this work cannot be ascribed at this time to any specific formation mechanism; biological, geological, and meteoritic sources of the organics observed are all possible. Further constraining the origin, distribution, and alteration history of the organic carbon observed at Cheyava Falls requires high-­resolution and high-­sensitivity analyses in terrestrial laboratories, which can be facilitated by the return of this sample to Earth.

MATERIALS AND METHODS SHERLOC The SHERLOC instrument is a DUV Raman spectrometer mounted to the robotic arm of the Perseverance rover, with two context imagers: the ACI—a 10.1-­μm/pixel monochromatic camera—and the WATSON camera (11). SHERLOC Raman and fluorescence hyperspectral map measurements are collected on natural and abraded surfaces. Abraded surfaces are generated with the arm-­mounted drill equipped with the abrasion bit, which exposes a subsurface target 50 mm in diameter and a few millimeters deep for instrument measurements. Both natural and abraded targets are cleared of dust and abrasion tailings by the gas Dust Removal Tool, which puffs compressed gaseous N2 onto the surface in multiple orientations before SHERLOC observations. The SHERLOC DUV NeCu laser irradiates a target with 248.6-­nm photons (as fine as a 110-­μm-­diameter annulus at the surface), generating Raman scattered photons and photons from fluorescence emission of minerals and organic compounds. These photons are collected by the ACI objective lens and injected into the spectrometer optical path and projected onto the 512 pixel–by–2148 pixel

CCD (charge-­coupled device) (11, 64). The first and last 50 columns of pixels are not illuminated. The spectrometer CCD is illuminated in an arc, enabling the CCD columns to be read out in discrete groups of CCD rows (referred to as spectral regions) to allow for variable gain adjustment and limit dark noise (64). Each spectrum region contains 2148 CCD pixels. After a single spectrum is collected, the scanner mirror focuses the laser to a new location on the surface, rastering over a commanded area to build a hyperspectral map.

WATSON WATSON is a copy of the MSL’s Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) camera (65), capable of acquiring full-­color images focused at infinity to microscopic scales (13 μm/pixel). Bright Angel observations included placing WATSON at working distances (i.e., the distance between the front lens and the image target) of approximately 4 to 40 cm, providing an image resolution from ∼21 to 150 μm/pixel and a field of view that ranges from ~2.5 × 3.3 cm to 18 × 24 cm (11, 66). The rover’s robotic arm can position WATSON to acquire image mosaics, nested image suites of increasing spatial resolution, stereo pair images, and multiposition images for Structure from Motion quantitative surface relief products [(11) and references therein]. WATSON images can be stitched together to create rover self-­portraits and images are also used to colorize grayscale SHERLOC ACI images, yielding a high-­resolution blended composite that captures both texture and color information (67).

Mastcam-­Z Mast Camera Zoom (Mastcam-­Z or ZCAM) is a high-­heritage imaging system based on MSL’s Mastcam, capable of acquiring high-­ resolution panoramic, stereoscopic, and color/multispectral context images of the martian surface (68). Mastcam-­Z consists of a pair of focusable, 4:1 zoomable cameras that provide broadband red/green/ blue and narrowband 400-­ to 1000-­nm color imaging. The cameras can resolve ∼0.7-­mm features at 2 m and ∼3.3-­cm features at 100 m distance, for features ≥5 pixels in size (68). Mastcam-­Z images in Fig. 1 are radiometrically corrected color balanced to show natural color. The Planetary Data System (PDS) file names for images used are provided in table S4.

Spectroscopy data acquisition SHERLOC measurements are collected on natural surface targets and abraded patches after sunset, at favorably cold temperatures to limit the detector’s dark noise. ACI images presented in this manuscript are focus-­stack composite products, which are ground-­generated images incorporating the best-­focus regions within the field of view after aligning the stack of images to correct for lateral offsets. All SHERLOC spectroscopy measurements presented in this manuscript are “detail” scans: 10 × 10 point maps, with 100-­μm spacing between points, and 900 laser pulses at each point. On sol 1024, the SHERLOC ACI focus mechanism experienced a failure that prevented operation of the instrument’s autofocus capability. Anomaly recovery activities resulted in a static fixed-­focus instrument that can be successfully focused using robotic arm positioning. Perseverance’s robotic arm is capable of placing SHERLOC normal to the target with an accuracy of <0.3 mm, depending on the mode of operation used for the target measurement, and retreating from the surface in steps of <0.25 mm. Focus offset effects on Raman D-­ and G-­bands Focus effects on Raman D-­ and G-­band signals were explored in the laboratory with the SHERLOC Brassboard analog instrument at NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory on several synthetic and natural samples including Murchison meteorite shown in fig. S6B. Further, on sol 1256, SHERLOC analyzed the SaU 008 meteorite calibration target aboard the rover and collected spectra at focus and 1.52 mm out of focus to replicate similar focus offsets during Bright Angel data collection (Fig. 4). Laboratory focus test results showed that when the targets are out of focus by ~1.14 mm, the Raman G-­band intensity decreases by ~50 to 61%, and the G-­band FWHM increases by ~9 to 15 cm−1. The focus offset experiment on Mars resulted in a ~35% decrease in the signal-­to-­noise ratio (SNR) of the SaU 008 pyroxene peak at 1009 cm−1 and showed that out-­of-­focus measurements attenuate the spectral intensity of Raman D-­ and G-­bands by approximately 35%. SHERLOC’s SNR coupled with a decrease in signal intensity make it difficult to determine the presence or absence of a D-­band. Table 1 summarizes the spectroscopy measurements and associated focus plane offsets for each Bright Angel measurements discussed in this work.

Spectroscopy data processing methods SHERLOC data presented in this manuscript are processed with Python scripts using standard Python modules as described below. Spectral data are read from the CCD and binned vertically according to the CCD regions defined (11). Three spectral regions were used for data collected in this manuscript, and all processing below is applied only to “region 1”—the Raman region (800 to 4000 cm−1) of the detector. Spectral “region 2” and “region 3” make up the fluorescence region (~265 to ~355 nm) and are discussed in the “Fluorescence” section of the Supplementary Text. Active (CCD integration with laser firing) and dark (CCD integration with the laser disabled)

spectra are collected in sequence at each spatial point on the surface, and the dark spectrum is used to subtract the spectral background from the active spectrum. Spectra are then filtered to remove data points collected at warm detector temperatures (Table 1), and cosmic rays are removed from spectral maps. Raman peak fitting and peak confidence calculations are performed on spectra following these data processing steps. Laser normalization and background subtraction processing steps each amplify spectral noise and are therefore not applied to most spectral processing in this manuscript, with exceptions described below. The SHERLOC optical background is effectively accounted for by deconvolving the fully constrained Si-­O peak with the ~1600-­cm−1 spectral feature. Below, we provide more detail on each of the steps outlined above. Spectrometer CCD temperature and dark noise The SHERLOC spectrometer CCD is passively cooled and transfers heat to a heatsink phase-­change material containing n-­decane (with a melting point of −30°C) to provide a stable thermal environment for spectroscopy measurements (11). Long measurements and operational restrictions resulted in some datasets collected in nonideal, warmer environments. The spectrometer CCD is nominally read out at −28°C for the entire hyperspectral map acquisition. The contribution of detector dark noise increases with increasing detector temperature and, in some cases, overwhelms the signal. The spectrometer CCD temperature is not reported with every point, but the temperature can be inferred from the median noise in the dark frame. We exclude all spectra collected with a median dark frame value higher than 1730 counts, which approximately corresponds to detector temperatures warmer than −28°C. Table 1 reports the temperature ranges that the CCD experienced during the scan and the number of spectra used in averaging. Laser normalization per map During a SHERLOC spectroscopy measurement, the laser and laser power supply gradually warm, producing fewer 248.6-­nm photons during each pulse. An internal laser photodiode measures the intensity variability of the laser signal for each pulse in a hyperspectral map acquisition, which can enable a spectral correction for relative laser intensity variability within a map, as described in Eq. 1, where Ii is the signal intensity for point i and pi is the photodiode intensity for point i. Peak fitting of Raman bands SHERLOC Raman band parameters presented in this manuscript are calculated from least squares fitting Gaussian functions to the optical background signal and G-­band in the spectral data. Laboratory Raman G-­band results are calculated from least squares fitting Gaussian functions using a single peak (G-­band) or by deconvolving multiple peaks with contributions from a D-­band (2 peaks), a D-­ band and an atmospheric O2 line (3 peaks), or a D-­band, O2 line, and carbonate ν3 peak (4 peaks) using the curve_fit function in the scipy.optimize package. The MMC structure consists of a mixture of sp2 and sp3 hybridized carbons bonded in a variety of organic structures with substituted heteroatoms (17). Because G-­bands derive from an amorphous solid that lacks spatial order and long-­range translational symmetry, the Raman spectrum observed originates from the vibrational density of states of the solid modified by the resonance Raman enhancement of each state (17). Therefore, the classical Gaussian, Lorentzian, and Voigt Raman band fitting functions do not model the physics of the MMC Raman spectrum, and any functional fit to the spectrum is a purely empirical method of quantitatively comparing MMC spectra (17, 71). Simpler fits are preferred, as more variables in the fit increases the number of solutions to the least squares algorithm and increases the uncertainty in the peak fit parameters. The peak fit parameters presented in Fig. 5 are derived from the observed Raman bands (72); currently, Raman bandwidth calibration techniques used to derive the intrinsic Raman band are only developed for homogeneously broadened bands (73), though the instrument slit function may also have an effect on heterogeneously broadening bands like that of the ~1600-­cm−1 feature (72). The terrestrial analog instruments have smaller slit functions than SHERLOC (34.1 cm−1), and therefore, the SHERLOC observed Raman band FWHM is expected to be higher than laboratory instruments, as demonstrated by the peak fit parameters of the HOPG measurements presented in Fig. 5. In addition to the >99% confidence of the ~1600-­cm−1 feature in the trimmed mean Apollo Temple spectrum, the sequence of target analyses further enhances our confidence in the detection of the candidate G-­band indicative of organics. Fused silica optical background The front optical element of SHERLOC, which is part of the instrument background signal, is a fused silica window that generates a weak band at ~1605 cm−1 attributable to an overtone of the 800-­cm−1 band of silica (70). The intensity ratio of the 1605/800 peaks in the fused silica background is ~0.07, while in the Apollo Temple spectra, this ratio is ~0.52; thus, the fused silica background might contribute to the ~1600-­cm−1 feature, but it is not strong enough to account for the majority of the ~1600-­cm−1 feature. Another phase must be responsible for this feature. Mineral contributions Numerous minerals exhibit minor Raman overtone modes in the 1600-­cm−1 region; however, associated fundamental vibrational modes would be expected to exhibit higher intensity peaks. For example, carbonate minerals have minor Raman modes at ν3 (at ~1443 cm−1) and ν1 + ν4 (~1763 cm−1), which are 9× to 48× less intense than the ν1 mode (~1080 to 1099 cm−1) (25, 76). Previous carbonate detections with SHERLOC on Mars have shown the ν1 mode but not the minor peaks (19, 27, 29); if carbonate were contributing to the ~1600-­cm−1 feature at Apollo Temple, we would expect a stronger corresponding feature for the ν1 mode, which is not observed. Amorphous minerals, such as amorphous carbonates and silicate glasses, have been shown to exhibit broad Raman features compared to crystalline minerals of the same composition (77). The possibility of broad, amorphous carbonate peaks in this region was considered, but visible Raman spectroscopy shows that amorphous carbonate peaks have relatively narrow bandwidths compared to that observed at Bright Angel, and do not exhibit the ν3 and ν1 + ν4 modes (78). The broadness of the ~1600-­cm−1 feature observed in Bright Angel rocks (>100 FWHM) compared to mineral Raman features (<50 FWHM, and based on SHERLOC’s slit width of ~34 cm−1) (64, 72) indicates that the Bright Angel ~1600-­cm−1 feature is not likely a mineral, or a combination of mineral modes. Hydrated minerals and hydroxyl group compounds can give rise to Raman bands in the 1600-­ to 1650-­cm−1 and 3200-­ to 3550-­cm−1 regions, due to H-­O-­H bending and O-­H stretching vibrations, respectively (79). Mineral hydration is characterized by a hydrogen stretching mode in the ~3000 to 3800 cm−1 spectral range, and H-­O-­H bending modes are very weak compared to the strong stretching mode vibrations (25). The Steamboat Mountain target exhibits a hydrated sulfate Raman signal, including a broad hydration stretching mode at ~3600 cm−1 and a bending mode at ~1646 (±10.1) cm−1 (fig. S2). Notably, there are no observed hydration stretching modes in the 3200-­ to 3550-­cm−1 region in any of the other targets at Bright Angel; thus, any contribution from bending modes in the 1600-­cm−1 region that could complicate the G-­band assignment are, in the upper limit, at the level of the noise in our measurements. Contamination Last, we note that terrestrial organic contamination is unlikely and does not adequately explain the observed diversity in G-­band signals across Apollo Temple, Cheyava Falls, and Walhalla Glades, or the absence of such signals in other martian rocks and SHERLOC calibration targets. The SHERLOC instrument never makes contact with the surface of a rock, and the abrasion bit used for Apollo Temple was cleaned and sterilized before launch (80) and is the same bit used on other abrasions in Jezero Crater, none of which exhibit the same band strength as that observed in Apollo Temple.

The topographic variability within detail maps in the Apollo Temple abrasion patch is <0.37 and <0.035 mm in the Walhalla Glades abrasion patch detail map, determined from ACI range map products (65).
